  "text": "Afterward she went home and found that she had left the kitchen light on.

It shone through the thin curtain onto the path. For a moment, coming through the gate, she expected her mother to be sitting at the table. Not alive again. Only sitting there, as she had so often been when Maren came in late.

There was no one. The cup beside the sink was her own.

She put the kettle on.

By spring the harbour wall needed pointing. Erris helped carry sand in a bucket too large for her, dragging its rim against her knee. Maren watched from the office doorway. Then she went inside and brought out a smaller bucket.

The girl took it without thanks. She was at the age when being understood was sometimes worse than being refused.

That evening she did not ask the time.

Maren heard her laughing farther down the street, among other voices, and went up alone.

There were things she began to keep at the lighthouse. Dry socks. Matches. A tin of biscuits that softened despite the lid. In the log she recorded a loose hinge, a cracked pane, the first swallow seen above the harbour.

Under her mother's last entry she had once written only the date and the hour.

Now the pages filled slowly.

One night she wrote that the sea was calm, then crossed it out. There had been a little wind from the east. She could hear the water working at the stones below.

She wrote that instead, and left room for tomorrow."

  "text": "In June someone mended the gate at the foot of the lighthouse path.

Maren found the old latch laid on the wall. The new one lifted easily. She tried it twice, then carried the old iron up with her, not knowing why it seemed wrong to leave it in the rain.

At ten past twelve she wound the clock three times.

The nights were hardly dark now. Through the cracked pane she could see the harbour roofs and a sheet left on somebody's line. Nothing moved except one corner of the sheet.

Her mother had known these nights too. Maren had always pictured her here in winter, bent over the mechanism with her coat still buttoned. It had not occurred to her that Agnes might sometimes have stood at the window because she liked the view.

The next afternoon Erris came to borrow a pencil.

Maren gave her one from the kitchen drawer.

'You can keep it,' she said.

'I only need it till Thursday.'

On Thursday the pencil returned, shorter and newly sharpened. Maren put it beside the log.

She never learned who had fixed the gate. By August the latch had begun to catch again. She took oil up in a small bottle and worked it into the hinge, opening and closing the gate until it swung without a sound.

There was still an hour before she was needed above.

She sat on the low wall. A boat was coming in, too far away to name. She stayed to see whose it was."

  "text": "The boat belonged to the man who delivered coal. She knew it by the blue door he had fitted across the cabin, a house door cut down badly.

He raised a hand as he passed the wall. She raised hers. Neither called out.

In September he left a sack beneath the lighthouse stairs. Maren found no bill. She moved it clear of the damp and swept up the black grains with a brush that had been her mother's.

There were still things of Agnes's she used without noticing. The brush. The bread tin. A spoon worn thin along one edge. Grief sometimes arrived only after the task was finished.

That night she carried a second chair upstairs. It caught at the turn, and she had to bring it down and try again with the legs pointing upward.

No one was expected. She put it beside the window anyway.

At ten past twelve she wound the clock three times. The handle resisted on the last turn, as it always did. She waited until she heard the next tick before letting go.

Below, someone was walking home with a torch. The light vanished behind the net shed and appeared again farther along the quay.

Maren opened the log. She wrote that the coal had come. Then she added that the gate was holding.

A draught stirred the preceding pages. She laid the old latch across them to keep her place and went downstairs for more wood.

When she came back, the room was as she had left it. Both chairs faced the harbour."
